course.title: Maths Foundations
course.description: Rearrange an equation and know why each move is allowed. Read a straight line off a graph, and read a graph back into an equation.
course.audience: An adult returning to algebra who is comfortable with whole-number arithmetic.

paragraphs: The expression 3 + 2m gives the fare, in pounds, for a taxi trip of m miles, whatever the value of m, and that is the point of algebra: a single line with a letter in it describes every case of a relationship at once. The letter stands for a number that has not been given, and you reason about that number through what the line says about it. Algebra is also the notation of science and computing, and it is difficult to read far in either without it.

The course has six lessons in two parts. The first three, Rearranging, teach you to read a letter as a number you have not yet been told, and then to find that number by doing the same thing to both sides of an equation and undoing its operations one at a time, in the right order. The last three, Straight lines, place pairs of numbers on a grid, measure how steep a line is, and finish by connecting a straight line to the equation that draws it.
Each lesson explains an idea before asking about it, so every question you meet draws only on what has already been shown.
outcomes: You'll be able to read an expression such as 3x − 4 as a calculation and work out its value for any number.
You'll be able to solve an equation such as 3x + 2 = 23 and say why each step keeps it true.
You'll be able to undo a calculation in the right order, including one with brackets.
You'll be able to find the gradient of a straight line from two points on it.
You'll be able to draw the line for y = mx + c and read its equation back off the line.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with whole-number arithmetic, which is all the course assumes.

lessons.title: What a letter stands for

lead.text: Suppose you are told that adding 8 to a certain number gives 14, and nothing else about it. Those two facts are enough to find the number, because every operation has an opposite that undoes it, and applying the opposite to the result runs the calculation backwards to the number it started from.

Subtraction undoes addition, so to reverse the adding of 8 you take 8 away from 14, which leaves 6. You can then check the answer by running the calculation forwards, since 6 + 8 is 14, the result you were given. In the figure, the upper row shows the calculation as it was done and the lower row shows it undone.

The same reasoning works when the number has been doubled. If doubling a number gives 18, you undo the doubling by halving, which gives 9, and the forward check confirms it, because double 9 is 18. The buttons on the figure switch between the two calculations.

Algebra is a way of writing statements like these, about a number known only through what was done to it, so that the same reasoning can be applied whatever the numbers are. Before you meet that notation, you can try one of these calculations yourself.

steps.headline: Giving the unknown number a name

lead.text: The statement you have just worked with can be written in words as “my number + 5 = 12”, but writing the words out on every line soon becomes clumsy. School arithmetic books often replace them with an empty box, which marks the place where the unknown number belongs:

The box says that some number goes in that place, and the statement asks which number fits. A box has two drawbacks, however: you cannot read it aloud, and a statement about two unknown numbers would need two boxes that look exactly alike. Algebra therefore writes a letter where the box was:

The letter is a name for the unknown number. It does not mean multiply, and it need not be x, since any letter would serve; the habit of choosing x goes back to René Descartes, who in 1637 used letters from the end of the alphabet for unknown quantities and letters from the beginning for known ones. A letter used in this way is called a **variable**, because in a different statement the same letter can stand for a different number.

A statement with an equals sign in the middle, such as x + 5 = 12, is called an **equation**. The part before the equals sign is its left side and the part after it is its right side, and the equation claims that the two sides come to the same number. Read aloud, it says “some number, with 5 added, makes 12”, which is the statement you began with.
So far the letter has stood only for a number you are trying to find, but it can also describe a calculation before any number has been chosen, and that is the subject of the next screen.

steps.headline: Putting a number in place of the letter

lead.text: Take x + 5 on its own, with no equals sign and no result to match. What remains is a calculation with a gap in it, an instruction to add 5 to whatever number x turns out to be, and a calculation written with a letter in this way is called an **expression**. An expression makes no claim, so it is neither true nor false; it simply has a value once a number is chosen for the letter.
The figure draws the expression x + 5 as a machine, which takes in a number on the left, adds 5 to it, and passes the result out on the right. Move the slider to choose the number that goes in.

afterFigure.text: With 3 as the input the machine gives 8, and with 10 it gives 15. Replacing the letter by a number in this way is called **substituting**, and each substitution tells you what the expression is worth for that particular number.

The target shown beside the output is 12, the right side of x + 5 = 12. If you move the slider until the output reaches it, the machine finds by trial the number you found earlier by working backwards. Trial is slower than reasoning, but it works for any expression at all, and it is the basis of the test for a solution later in this lesson.
The same letter can also appear more than once in an expression, as it does in x + x + 4, and the question then is whether each copy may stand for a different number.

lead.text: When a letter appears twice, both copies stand for the same number, because within a single expression a letter has one value throughout. The method is therefore to write the number in place of every copy of the letter first, and only then to do the arithmetic.

workedSteps.text: Write 5 in place of each x.
Work out the sum.

lead.text: In algebra a number written directly in front of a letter, with nothing between them, means that the two are multiplied, so 3x means 3 × x, or three lots of x. The convention appears on almost every line of algebra you will read, which is why it is worth learning now.

The multiplication sign is left out because × looks too much like the letter x, and in handwritten working the two are easily confused. The figure shows the machine for 3x, which multiplies whatever goes in by 3.

afterFigure.text: An input of 4 gives an output of 12, since 3 × 4 is 12. It does not give 34, which is what you would get by writing the digits 3 and 4 side by side, so whenever you substitute a number for the letter, the multiplication sign has to be written back in.

Three lots of x can also be written x + x + x, which agrees with the previous screen: x is one number, and 3x is that number taken three times. Only multiplication is left unwritten in this way, so in 3 + x the plus sign stays.
An expression such as 3x − 4 asks for two operations, a multiplication and a subtraction, and that raises the question of which one is done first.

lead.text: The expression 3x − 4 asks for two things to be done to x: multiply it by 3, and take away 4. The order in which you do them changes the result, as x = 5 shows. Multiplying first gives 15, and taking away 4 then leaves 11, whereas taking away 4 first gives 1, and multiplying that by 3 gives 3.

Since a line of algebra has to mean the same thing to everyone who reads it, mathematicians follow an agreed rule: multiplication is done before addition or subtraction, unless brackets say otherwise. Under that rule 3x − 4 means multiply first and then subtract, and the same rule makes 2 + 3 × 4 equal to 14, because 3 × 4 is worked out before the 2 is added.

afterFigure.text: The figure follows the agreed order from left to right. The input 5 enters the first box, which multiplies by 3 and gives 15, and the second box takes away 4 and gives 11, whereas doing the subtraction first would have given 3, which is not what 3x − 4 means. Any expression can be worked out in the same way, by listing its operations in the order the rule gives and recording what comes out of each.
With practice you will not need the boxes at all, because you will read 3x − 4 directly as “multiply by 3, then subtract 4”.

lead.text: Work through the two boxes in the order the rule gives.

reveal.text: Multiplication comes first, so 3 × 6 gives 18, and subtracting 4 from 18 then leaves 14.

lead.text: Return to x + 5 = 12. The machine showed that 7 fits it, and fitting has a precise meaning: when 7 is put in place of x, the left side becomes 7 + 5, which is 12, and the right side is 12 already, so the two sides are equal and the claim the equation makes is true.

A number that makes the two sides of an equation equal is called a **solution** of the equation, and finding it is called **solving** the equation. Testing whether a number is a solution takes three steps: substitute it for the letter, work out the left side, and compare the result with the right side.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the equation as a balance, with the left side in one pan and the right side in the other. At x = 4 the left pan holds 9 and the right pan holds 12, so the balance tips and 4 is not a solution, and as you slide x along, the balance comes level at only one value.
A solution has to make the two sides exactly equal, so a number that brings the left side to 11 or 13 tips the balance just as surely as one that brings it to 50.

lead.text: Apply the three steps of the test. The substitution has been done for you, and the calculation and the comparison are yours to complete.

workedSteps.text: Replace x with 4.
Calculate the left side.
Compare with the right side, 9.

lead.text: Here the same test is applied to a new equation. Work out the left side first, and then compare it with the right side.

reveal.text: Substituting 3 gives a left side of 13, one more than the right side, and since a solution must make the two sides exactly equal, 3 is not a solution of this equation.

lead.text: A taxi charges £3 at the start of a journey and £2 for every mile, so for a trip of m miles the fare in pounds is 3 + 2m. The expression is read with the same rule about order as before.

blocks.text: Consider the line 2x + 3 = 17. It is short, but it makes a precise claim: there is a number which, doubled and then increased by 3, comes to 17. The letter x stands for that number, whose value you have not been told, and the rest of the line records what was done to it and what came out.

Read in this way, algebra is far less forbidding than its letters suggest, because each line is a sentence about a number written in a compact notation that takes only a few minutes to learn. The letter does not hide anything; it gives the missing number a name, so that the number can be carried from one line of working to the next before anyone knows its value.

The rest of this course depends on reading lines like this one. Solving an equation, which the next two lessons do step by step, means finding the one number that makes its claim true, and drawing a straight line from its equation means finding every pair of numbers that does. Both begin with the skill you will learn here, which is putting a number in place of the letter and seeing whether the claim holds.

intro.promise: By the end you will read 3x − 4 as a calculation waiting for a number, and you will be able to test whether a given number solves an equation.

recap.keyIdea: A letter stands for one number throughout an expression, and a number solves an equation only when substituting it makes the two sides exactly equal.

blocks.text: An equation such as x + 5 = 12 claims that its two sides are equal, and 7 is its solution because substituting it gives 12 on both sides. Expressions such as 3x − 4 and 3 + 2m are worked out by substituting the number and then multiplying before adding or subtracting, and the test for a solution follows the same order, which is why 3 fails for 5x − 2 = 12: its left side comes to 13.

recap.nextHook: Testing numbers finds a solution only if you happen to try the right one, and for 5x − 2 = 12 no whole number works. The next lesson uses a balance to find the solution directly, and shows why each step of the method is allowed.

lessons.title: Keeping the balance

lead.text: The figure shows a pair of scales with a tied bag and 6 loose marbles in the left pan and 10 marbles in the right, and the pans are level. Every marble weighs the same, so the scales make a claim much like an equation: the bag together with 6 marbles weighs as much as 10 marbles. If you lift the 6 loose marbles out of the left pan alone, that pan rises and the scales tip, but if you also take 6 marbles from the right pan, they settle level again.

The left pan now holds only the bag and the right pan holds the 4 marbles that remain of the 10, and since the scales are level, the bag must weigh the same as 4 marbles. You have found what the bag holds without opening it.

The method depends on one fact about equal amounts: if you take the same quantity from each, what remains is still equal. The same holds when you add the same quantity to each, or double or halve both, whereas a change made to one pan alone breaks the balance, and anything you then conclude about the bag is wrong.

An equation is a statement that two amounts are equal, so every change that keeps the scales level also keeps an equation true. You can try the method on a second pair of scales before seeing it written as an equation.

lead.text: As before, every marble weighs the same and the pans are level, so you can find the bag's contents by removing the same number of marbles from both pans.

reveal.text: Removing the 3 loose marbles from both pans leaves the bag on one side and the marbles it balances on the other. The next screen writes that move as an equation.

lead.text: The scales can now be written down. If x stands for the number of marbles in the bag, the left pan holds x and 3 loose marbles and the right pan holds 11, so the level scales say:

The two pans are the two sides of the equation, and the equals sign says that they weigh the same. Taking 3 from both sides leaves x on its own on the left and 11 − 3 on the right, which is the move you made with the marbles, and it gives x = 8.

afterFigure.text: A one-sided move shows why both sides matter. If you take 3 from the left side alone, you are left with x = 11, but substituting 11 into the original equation gives a left side of 14 against a right side of 11, because the one-sided move turned the equation into a different one with a different solution.

Doing the same thing to both sides, by contrast, produces a new equation with exactly the same solution as the old one, and a simpler equation with the same solution is precisely what you want when solving.

lead.text: The balance shows 2x + 6 on the left and 18 on the right. Choose the move that turns this into a simpler equation with exactly the same solution.

reveal.text: A move keeps the solution only if it acts on both sides. Subtracting 6 from each side turns 2x + 6 = 18 into 2x = 12, which has the same solution and a simpler form.

lead.text: The scales tell you which moves are allowed but not which one to make. To choose, look at what has been done to x and undo it, so that in an equation such as 3x = 12, where x has been multiplied by 3, the move to make is the one that reverses that multiplication.

If 5 has been added to a number, taking 5 away gives back the number, so adding and subtracting undo each other. Multiplying and dividing undo each other in the same way, since a number multiplied by 3 and then divided by 3 is the number you started with.

A move that undoes another in this way is called its **inverse operation**, and on the scales it has a clear meaning. Suppose three identical bags balance 12 marbles, which is the equation 3x = 12 shown in the figure. Dividing both sides by 3 splits each pan into three equal parts, and one bag then balances 4 marbles.

afterFigure.text: The general method, then, is to find what has been done to x and apply the inverse operation to both sides. One move is never allowed, which is dividing by 0, because nothing undoes multiplying by 0: every number multiplied by 0 gives 0, so there is no way back to the number you started with.
The slider lets you test other values of x against 3x = 12, and only one of them brings the balance level.

lead.text: In 4x = 20 the letter x has been multiplied by 4. Decide which inverse operation undoes that, and apply it to both sides.

reveal.text: The inverse of × 4 is ÷ 4, and applying it to both sides leaves x alone in a single move.

lead.text: Most equations need more than one move. If four identical bags and 3 loose marbles sit in the left pan and 19 marbles sit in the right, the equation is:

The left pan cannot be split into four equal parts while the loose marbles are mixed in with the bags, so the loose marbles have to come off first, and the same number must come off the right pan. Subtracting 3 from both sides leaves four bags balancing 16 marbles:

afterFigure.text: Now the pan can be split. Dividing both sides by 4 leaves one bag balancing 4 marbles, so x = 4, and the test from the first lesson confirms it: substituting 4 into the original equation gives a left side of 4 × 4 + 3 = 19, which matches the right side.
The next example writes the same two moves as a column of equations, naming the inverse operation at each line.

lead.text: Here the moves are written as equations. Each line names the move, applies it to both sides, and shows the equation that results.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 from both sides. It undoes the + 2.
Now the × 3 has to go. Which move undoes it?
Divide both sides by 3.
Check in the original equation.

lead.text: The first move is done for you, and the last two lines are yours to complete.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 8 from both sides.
Divide both sides by 2. Which x makes 2x = 12 true?
Check in the original equation.

steps.headline: When the numbers go below zero

lead.text: Take 2x − 4 = −10, which has a subtraction on the left and a negative number on the right. The same two ideas apply as before: 4 has been taken away from 2x, the inverse of taking away is adding, and so the first move is to add 4 to both sides.

The left side becomes 2x and the right side becomes −10 + 4. A thermometer makes this sum easy to picture, since a reading of 10 degrees below zero that rises by 4 degrees ends at 6 below zero, so −10 + 4 = −6 and the equation now reads 2x = −6.

afterFigure.text: Dividing both sides by 2 finishes the solution. Since a negative number divided by a positive number is negative, −6 divided by 2 is −3, so x = −3, and substituting −3 into the original equation confirms it: 2 × (−3) is −6, and −6 − 4 is −10, which matches the right side.
A negative solution is as valid as any other, because nothing in the method requires x to be positive, and the balance in the figure levels at x = −3 just as it would at a positive value.

lead.text: In 3x − 9 = −15, the 9 is taken away from 3x and the right side is negative. Decide which move undoes the subtraction, and check your answer in the original equation.

lessons.orientation: Justify each step of a rearrangement by naming the operation applied to both sides.
lessons.nextAction: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.

blocks.text: At the end of the last lesson, the equation 5x − 2 = 12 resisted every whole number you could try, because its solution is 2.8. Testing values can confirm a solution once you have one, but it cannot be relied on to find one, and an equation like this needs a method that leads to the answer directly.

The method rests on a single observation about equal quantities, which is easiest to see on a pair of scales. If two pans balance and you take the same weight from each, they still balance, whereas taking weight from one pan alone tips them. An equation behaves in the same way, since its two sides are equal amounts, and it stays true under exactly the changes that keep a pair of scales level.

That observation is all the justification the method needs. Each step in solving an equation does the same thing to both sides, chosen so that it undoes one of the operations applied to x, and when the last of them has been undone, x stands alone with its value on the other side.

intro.promise: By the end you will know why doing the same thing to both sides keeps an equation true, and you will use that fact to solve for x.

recap.keyIdea: An equation stays true when you do the same thing to both sides, so you can undo the operations applied to x, one inverse at a time, until x stands alone.

blocks.text: Taking the same amount from both pans keeps a pair of scales level, and an equation obeys the same rule, so 3x + 2 = 23 became 3x = 21 when 2 was subtracted from both sides, and x = 7 when both sides were divided by 3. Negative numbers change nothing in the method, which is why adding 9 to both sides of 3x − 9 = −15 led, after one more division, to x = −2.

recap.nextHook: In every example so far the order of the moves was given to you. The next lesson explains why that order is the right one, and how to solve an equation in which x is wrapped in several operations, including a pair of brackets.

lessons.title: Undoing in the right order

lead.text: Take the equation 3x − 9 = 21, which says that a number trebled and then reduced by 9 gives 21. The last operation was taking away 9, so it is undone first, and 21 + 9 is 30. The operation before it was trebling, so it is undone next, and 30 divided by 3 is 10.

afterFigure.text: The figure runs the calculation forwards: 10 trebled is 30, and taking away 9 gives 21, which meets the target. Undoing the operations in the order they were done would fail, because dividing 21 by 3 first and then adding 9 gives 16, and 16 trebled with 9 taken away is 39, not 21.

Whatever was done last has to be undone first, and each operation is undone by its inverse, so reading a calculation from its result back to its start recovers the number it began with. Solving an equation that needs several moves comes down to exactly this.

lead.text: This calculation also has two operations. Start from the result and undo them, last one first.

reveal.text: The 4 was added last, so it comes off first, and the doubling is undone after it. The next screen shows how to read the order of the operations from an equation.

steps.headline: Reading the operations from an equation

lead.text: Take 2x + 5 = 11. The rule from the first lesson, that multiplication comes before addition, tells you how to read the left side: start with x, double it, and then add 5, and the equation says that the result of those operations is 11.

afterFigure.text: Working backwards from 11, the last operation was adding 5, so taking 5 away gives 6, and the operation before it was doubling, so halving 6 gives 3. The machine in the figure confirms it, since an input of 3 produces 11.

On the scales, those two backward steps are the two moves of the last lesson: subtract 5 from both sides, then divide both sides by 2. The moves come in the reverse of the order in which the operations were applied, so reading the left side tells you where to begin.

lead.text: Begin by reading the operations: 5x − 3 means multiply by 5 and then take away 3. Taking away 3 was done last, so it is the first to undo.

workedSteps.text: The last job was − 3, so add 3 to both sides first.
Then undo the × 5: divide both sides by 5.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Read the operations applied to x, and then undo them, last one first. The first line asks you to choose the route, and the lines after it carry the route out.

workedSteps.text: Read the jobs on x in 2x + 3, then choose the route that undoes them.
Subtract 3 from both sides. It undoes the last job.
Divide both sides by 2.
Check by running the machine forward.

lead.text: Identify the operation applied last, undo it on both sides, and then undo the one before it.

reveal.text: The operations were undone in the reverse of the order in which the expression applies them: first the subtraction, then the multiplication.

lead.text: In 3(x + 2), the brackets are the curved marks around x + 2, and they tell you to work out what is inside them first and to treat the result as a single quantity. A number written directly in front of a bracket means multiply, just as it does in 3x, so in 3(x + 2) the 2 is added to x first and the whole of x + 2 is then multiplied by 3.

afterFigure.text: The figure applies the operations in that order, so an input of 4 becomes 6 inside the brackets and 18 after the multiplication. Multiplying by 3 is therefore the last operation and the first to undo: you divide both sides by 3, which removes the brackets, and then take away the 2. In 3x + 2, by contrast, the 2 sits outside the multiplication and is added last, so the brackets have changed which operation comes last.
The same method works however many layers an expression has. List its operations in the order the expression applies them, starting inside the brackets, and then undo them from the other end.

lead.text: Find the operation applied last in 3(x + 2), undo it first, and then deal with what is inside the brackets.

reveal.text: The 3 multiplies everything inside the brackets, so dividing by 3 comes first, and taking away the 2 comes second.

steps.headline: Answers that are not whole numbers

lead.text: In the first lesson you tested 3 in 5x − 2 = 12 and found a left side of 13, one too many, and in fact no whole number fits this equation. The method now finds its solution directly: the last operation in 5x − 2 is taking away 2, so adding 2 to both sides gives 5x = 14, and dividing both sides by 5 comes next.

afterFigure.text: Since 14 does not divide evenly by 5, the solution is the fraction 14/5, which is 2.8 as a decimal. Running the calculation forwards confirms it, because 5 × 2.8 is 14 and 14 − 2 is 12, and if you slide the input in the figure to 2.8, the output meets the target.

Nothing in the method requires a whole-number answer, so when the final division does not come out even, you write the solution as a fraction or a decimal. A fraction such as 14/5 is exact, whereas a decimal is sometimes only a rounded version of a fraction, as 0.33 is of 1/3.

lead.text: Division is an operation like any other: x ÷ 4 means x divided into four equal parts, and multiplying by 4 undoes it. Undo each operation with its inverse, last one first.

lessons.orientation: Unwind an expression by reversing the order its operations were applied in.

blocks.text: The expression 2x + 3 describes two operations applied to a number in a fixed order: the number is doubled, and then 3 is added to the result. To recover the number from a known result, you have to take those operations off again, and the order in which you take them off is decided by the order in which they went on.

In 2x + 3 the addition of 3 was applied last, so it is the first operation you can reach, since everything else lies underneath it, and in general the operations come off in the reverse of the order in which they were applied. The examples in the last lesson followed this rule when they told you which move to make first, and once you can see why it works, you can choose the order yourself for any equation.

The rule matters most where the order is hard to see at a glance, as in an expression such as 3(x + 2), where brackets change which operation is applied last, and in equations whose solutions are not whole numbers, which no amount of trial would find.

intro.promise: By the end you will undo a calculation one operation at a time, last operation first, to find the number it started from.

recap.keyIdea: To find x, undo the operations in reverse order, last one first, doing the same thing to both sides at every step.

blocks.text: Because the last operation applied to x is the first one you can reach, 5x − 3 = 12 was solved by adding 3 and then dividing by 5, and 3(x + 2) = 21 by dividing by the 3 outside the brackets before taking off the 2. The same method gave x = 2.8 for 5x − 2 = 12, a solution that trying whole numbers could never have reached.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts numbers onto a grid, where a pair of them fixes a single point.

lessons.title: A point is a pair

lead.text: In the figure, a square grid covers the page, and the point where the two heavier lines cross is the starting point for every position. That point is called the **origin**, and you reach any other point from it by moving across to the right and then up, counting grid squares along each part of the move.
The two counts are written in brackets with a comma between them, so (3, 2) means 3 across and 2 up, and the origin itself is (0, 0), since reaching it needs no movement at all.

afterFigure.text: The point labelled A in the figure is (3, 2): count three squares to the right of the origin and then two squares up, and you arrive at it. Every point on the grid has exactly one pair and every pair names exactly one point, so the pair works as the point's address.
Because one number is measured across and the other up, the order in which they are written matters, and swapping them generally names a different point.

lead.text: Compare (4, 1) with (1, 4). The first means 4 across and 1 up and the second means 1 across and 4 up, and the two moves end at points some distance apart, so a pair has to be written in a fixed order that everyone follows: across first, then up.

The first number, which counts squares across, is called the **x-coordinate**, and the second, which counts squares up, is called the **y-coordinate**; together they are the **coordinates** of the point. In (4, 1), the x-coordinate is 4 and the y-coordinate is 1.

afterFigure.text: The figure marks P at (4, 1) and Q at (1, 4), which use the same two numbers and land on different points. The order is easy to remember, because x comes before y in the alphabet just as the move across comes before the move up.
With the order settled, you can place any point from its pair by making the move across first and the move up second.

lead.text: Start at the origin, make the move across that the first number gives, and then make the move up that the second number gives.

reveal.text: The first number gives the move across and the second the move up, so writing the pair the other way round would put B at a different point.

lead.text: The two points in this question use the same numbers in opposite orders. Compare them one coordinate at a time.

reveal.text: The x-coordinates differ by one and so do the y-coordinates, so the two points are a step across and a step down apart, which is what swapping the numbers does.

steps.headline: Left of and below the origin

lead.text: The point R in the figure lies to the left of the origin, where no move to the right can reach it, and S lies below it. The number line shows how to describe such points, since on it the numbers below zero lie to the left of zero, so a minus sign can stand for the opposite direction.

A negative x-coordinate means move left instead of right, and a negative y-coordinate means move down instead of up. R = (−5, 2) is therefore 5 squares left of the origin and 2 up, and S = (3, −4) is 3 squares right and 4 down.

afterFigure.text: The sign belongs to its own number and changes only the direction of that part of the move, while the size of the number still counts squares. A point with two minus signs, such as (−2, −3), lies to the left of the origin and below it, and you reach it in the same way as any other, by a move across followed by a move up or down, with both going the opposite way.

lead.text: This pair has a minus sign in its first number, and the point is placed one coordinate at a time.

workedSteps.text: Start at the origin.
The x-coordinate is −4. Move 4 across, to the left.
The y-coordinate is 1. Move 1 up.
The x-coordinate is 4, so move 4 to the right.
Read the second number. What is the y-coordinate?
A y-coordinate of −2 means 2 squares down from there.

lead.text: The first number of the pair gives the position across, and its sign is part of it.

reveal.text: A minus sign on the x-coordinate means the point lies left of the origin, and the sign stays part of the coordinate.

lead.text: Two of the grid lines pass through the origin and matter more than the rest. The horizontal one is called the **x-axis** and the vertical one the **y-axis**, and each is a number line of its own, marked in squares outward from the origin.

A point on the x-axis has not moved up or down at all, so its y-coordinate is 0, as E = (−4, 0) shows, and a point on the y-axis has not moved across, so its x-coordinate is 0, as with F = (0, 3). The origin lies on both axes, which is why both of its coordinates are 0.

afterFigure.text: With the axes named, you can follow any pair to its point and read the pair back from any point, and the last question asks for both, for a point that lies below and to the left of the origin.

lead.text: A point lies at (−2, −3), and you start from the origin, (0, 0). You may move only along the grid lines, first across and then up or down.

lessons.orientation: Place a point from its coordinates and read coordinates back off a plotted point.

blocks.text: The pair of numbers (3, 2) is enough to pick out a single point on a flat surface: start from an agreed point, move 3 units to the right and then 2 units up, and you arrive at exactly one place. Two numbers are needed because a flat surface extends in two directions, across and up, while a single number can fix a position only along one line.

Maps, chess boards and the screen you are reading all name their places with two numbers in this way. The method of describing points by numbers, so that lines and curves can be studied through equations, goes back to the work of René Descartes and Pierre de Fermat in the 1630s, and it is where this course is heading, since its last two lessons draw straight lines from their equations.
Before any of that, a pair has to be read correctly, which means knowing which of its numbers is measured across and which up, and what a minus sign does to the direction of each.

intro.promise: By the end you will find any point on a grid from a pair of numbers, and write down the pair for any point you can see.

recap.keyIdea: A point is a pair (x, y), with x measured across and y measured up, and a minus sign turns the move to the left or down.

blocks.text: The pair (3, 2) means 3 across and 2 up from the origin, and swapping the numbers moves the point to a different place, because the first coordinate always measures across. Signs give direction, so (−4, 1) lies 4 to the left and 1 up, the y-coordinate of (4, −2) is −2, and reaching (−2, −3) along the grid lines takes 5 squares.

recap.nextHook: Two points joined with a ruler give a line, and every line slopes by some amount. The next lesson puts a number on how steep that slope is.

lessons.title: How steep is it

lead.text: To compare the two paths, divide each climb by the horizontal distance over which it happens. The shorter path climbs 30 metres over 15 metres, so it gains 30 ÷ 15 = 2 metres of height for each metre across, while the longer path spreads the same 30 metres over 60 metres and gains 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 metres for each metre across.

Since 2 is four times 0.5, the shorter path is four times as steep. The number obtained by dividing the climb by the horizontal distance is called the **gradient**, so a gradient of 2 means that the path climbs 2 metres for every 1 metre it covers horizontally.
The same division measures the steepness of a hill, a ramp, a roof or a line on a grid, provided you can find the climb and the horizontal distance.
Divide the climb by the horizontal distance, as you did for the two paths.

reveal.text: The climb divided by the horizontal distance is the gradient of the path, and the next screen carries the same division onto the grid.

steps.headline: Rise and run on the grid

lead.text: On a grid, the climb and the horizontal distance are measured with coordinates. If you pick two points on a line and move from the first to the second, the change in y is called the **rise** and the change in x is called the **run**, and the gradient is the rise divided by the run.
In the figure the line passes through A = (1, 2) and B = (4, 5). Moving from A to B, x goes from 1 to 4, so the run is 4 − 1 = 3, and y goes from 2 to 5, so the rise is 5 − 2 = 3.

afterFigure.text: Since the rise and the run are both 3, the gradient is 3 ÷ 3 = 1, and the line climbs one square for every square it moves across. You do not need the figure to find these numbers, because subtracting the coordinates of the two points gives the rise and the run directly; the figure only shows what each subtraction means.

lead.text: Read the y-coordinates of the two points. The rise is how far y increases as you move from A to B.

reveal.text: That change in y is the rise, and dividing it by the run gives the gradient.

lead.text: Take the points (2, 3) and (5, 9). The rise is the second point's y-coordinate minus the first point's, 9 − 3 = 6, and the run is found in the same way from the x-coordinates, 5 − 2 = 3, so the gradient is 6 ÷ 3 = 2. The subtraction works for any two points, however far apart they are, so you never need to count squares.

Both subtractions have to be taken in the same order. If you reverse only one of them, the gradient comes out with the wrong sign, so that a rise of 6 over a run of −3 gives −2, although the line in fact climbs. Taking each subtraction from the first point to the second ensures that both describe the same movement.
The next example carries a pair of points through the whole calculation, one line at a time.

workedSteps.text: Rise: subtract the y-coordinates, second minus first.
Run: subtract the x-coordinates in the same order.
Divide the rise by the run.
Rise: second y minus first y.
Run: second x minus first x.
Divide the rise by the run.

lead.text: Take the points C = (0, 6) and D = (3, 0) in the figure. Moving from C to D, y drops from 6 to 0, so the rise is 0 − 6 = −6, while the run is 3 − 0 = 3, which gives a gradient of −6 ÷ 3 = −2.

A negative rise means that the line goes down, so the sign of the gradient tells you which way the line slopes: a line that climbs as you move to the right has a positive gradient, and a line that falls has a negative one. A level line has a rise of 0, and 0 divided by any run is 0, so its gradient is 0.

afterFigure.text: The size of the gradient, ignoring its sign, tells you how steep the line is. A gradient of 3 climbs more steeply than a gradient of 1/2, just as the shorter path climbed more steeply than the longer one, and a gradient of −3 falls exactly as steeply as a gradient of 3 climbs.

lead.text: This line falls as it moves to the right. Take both subtractions in the same order and keep track of the signs.

reveal.text: The rise is negative and the run positive, so the gradient is negative, as the falling line suggests.

lead.text: This line is less steep than those before it. Keep the rise and the run separate until the final division.

lessons.orientation: Calculate a gradient from two points and say what its sign means.
lessons.nextAction: Draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and recover them from a drawn line.

blocks.text: A path that climbs 30 metres over 15 metres of horizontal distance is far steeper than one that climbs the same 30 metres over 60 metres, although both end at the same height. Neither the climb nor the distance gives the steepness on its own, because steepness depends on the two together, on how much height is gained for each metre travelled across.

The same is true of any straight line on a grid, which climbs or falls by some amount for each unit it moves across. A single number that captures this lets you compare lines exactly, where words such as “steep” and “gentle” describe them only roughly.
That number is defined by one division, and once you can calculate it from the coordinates of two points, its sign also tells you whether a line rises, falls or stays level.

intro.promise: By the end you will find a line's gradient from two of its points, and say what the sign of the gradient tells you.

recap.keyIdea: The gradient of a line is its rise divided by its run, both taken in the same direction, and its sign shows whether the line rises, falls or, with a gradient of 0, stays level.

blocks.text: Dividing the climb by the horizontal distance measures steepness, and on a grid the climb and the distance become the rise and the run, so the line through (1, 2) and (3, 12) has a gradient of 10 ÷ 2 = 5. The line through (−2, 3) and (2, −1) falls as it moves to the right, which is why its gradient, −1, is negative.

recap.nextHook: A gradient says how steeply a line slopes, but two lines with the same gradient can run side by side at different heights. The next lesson shows what fixes the position of a line, and how its gradient and its position combine in a single equation.

lessons.title: From equation to line

lead.text: At the start the candle is 12 centimetres tall. After 1 hour it has lost 2 centimetres and stands at 10, and after 2 hours it has lost 4 and stands at 8.

The height falls by 2 centimetres for every hour that passes, so after any number of hours the candle has lost 2 times that number, and the height that remains is the starting 12 minus that loss. After 5 hours, for instance, the loss is 2 × 5 = 10, and the candle stands at 12 − 10 = 2 centimetres.

If x is the number of hours and y is the height, as on the grid in the last two lessons, the rule becomes y = 12 − 2x. It contains just two numbers: the 12, where the candle starts, and the 2, which says how fast it burns.
Use the rule from the last screen, taking what has burned away from the starting height.

reveal.text: In 3 hours the candle loses 3 × 2 = 6 centimetres of its 12. The next screen plots these heights on a graph.

lead.text: Plotting the heights, with hours across and height up, gives one point for each hour: (1, 10) after 1 hour, (2, 8) after 2 hours, and so on down to (5, 2). The grid in the figure is only 10 squares high, so the points begin at the first hour, but the pattern continues beyond the edge.

afterFigure.text: The points lie on a straight line. Each hour across takes the height down by 2, so the line's gradient is −2, which is the burning rate with a minus sign because the height falls, and if you follow the line back to the y-axis, it crosses at 12, the candle's height when it was lit.

The height at which a line crosses the y-axis is called its **intercept**. Two numbers therefore fix the candle's line: the gradient says how steeply it slopes, and the intercept says where it crosses the y-axis.

steps.headline: Writing the line as an equation

lead.text: With these two numbers, the candle's line is y = −2x + 12, where −2 is the gradient and 12 is the intercept. Any straight line that is not vertical can be written in the same way with its own numbers, so the general pattern is written with letters as y = mx + c, in which m stands for the gradient and c for the intercept.

To see why c is the intercept, put x = 0 into the equation. The term mx becomes m × 0, which is 0, so y is simply c, and the point (0, c), which lies on the y-axis, is on the line. The line y = 3x + 4, for example, crosses the y-axis at height 4 and climbs 3 for every unit across.
The line meets the y-axis where x is 0, so put x = 0 into the equation.

reveal.text: With x = 0 the x-term disappears, so y is just the constant c, which is the intercept.

steps.headline: Drawing a line from its equation

lead.text: Take the equation y = 2x − 3. Choosing x = 0 and substituting gives y = 2 × 0 − 3 = −3, so the point (0, −3) lies on the line, and choosing x = 3 gives y = 2 × 3 − 3 = 3, so (3, 3) lies on it too. Any value of x produces a point in the same way, by substituting it and working out y with the multiplication done first.

afterFigure.text: Two points are enough, because only one straight line passes through both, so you can join them with a ruler and extend the line in either direction. The gradient between the two points provides a check: (3 − (−3)) ÷ 3 = 2, which is the 2 in the equation.
Substitution also works in the other direction. If y = 2x and you know that y is 14, then 2x = 14, and dividing both sides by 2 gives x = 7.

steps.headline: Find two points on y = 3x − 1, then draw the line.

workedSteps.text: Choose x = 0. This gives the intercept.
Choose x = 2.
Check the gradient from the two points.

steps.headline: Find the point on y = −x + 3 where x = 2.

workedSteps.text: Replace x with 2. The minus sign stays in front.
Work it out. What is y?

steps.headline: Reading the equation off a line

lead.text: Take the line in the figure, which passes through G = (0, 5) and H = (2, 1). The point on the y-axis, (0, 5), gives the intercept at once, so c = 5, and the gradient comes from the rise and the run between the two points: the rise is 1 − 5 = −4 and the run is 2 − 0 = 2, so m = −4 ÷ 2 = −2.

afterFigure.text: The line is therefore y = −2x + 5, and substituting the other point confirms it, since x = 2 gives y = −2 × 2 + 5 = 1, which matches (2, 1). A falling line always has a negative m, as the candle's line did.

lead.text: Read c from the point where x is 0, and then use both points to find the gradient.

reveal.text: The point on the y-axis gives c and the two points together give m, and those two numbers make up the whole equation.

lead.text: A container holds 2 litres at the start and gains 0.5 litres every minute, so after x minutes it holds y = 0.5x + 2 litres. The intercept is the starting amount and the gradient is the rate at which it fills.

blocks.text: A candle that is 12 centimetres tall and burns down by 2 centimetres every hour has heights of 12, 10, 8 and 6 centimetres at the start and after each of the next three hours. The whole list, however far it is continued, follows from two numbers: the starting height and the rate at which the height falls.

Those two numbers answer the question the last lesson left open. A gradient says how steeply a line slopes but not where it sits, and two lines with the same gradient can run side by side at different heights, so a line needs a second number, its height at the start, to fix it in place.

Plotted on a grid, the candle's heights lie on a straight line, and the equation of that line has the same form as the equation of almost every other straight line, which lets you draw a line from its equation and read the equation back from a line.

intro.promise: By the end you will draw the line of y = mx + c from its two numbers, and read both numbers back from a line.

recap.keyIdea: A line y = mx + c is fixed by two numbers: c, where it crosses the y-axis, and m, its gradient.

blocks.text: A candle that starts at 12 centimetres and burns 2 an hour has its heights on the line y = −2x + 12, whose intercept is the starting height and whose gradient is the rate with a minus sign. Substituting two values of x drew y = 3x − 1 through (0, −1) and (2, 5), and reading the intercept and the gradient from the line through (0, −2) and (2, 2) gave its equation, y = 2x − 2.
